sub_answers.sub_question: Does the second law or generalized free energy constraints forbid creating coherence without net work, and what formulations apply?
What are debated roles of catalysts, coherence reservoirs, and reference frames in enabling otherwise forbidden transformations?
sub_answers.text: Catalytic coherence transformations can enable otherwise forbidden incoherent operations and there are necessary and sufficient conditions characterizing deterministic and stochastic catalytic transformations between pure states [d30133s0p0]. Self-catalysis, where a system can act as its own catalyst for coherence transformations, is possible in some cases [d30133s0p0]. Catalytic or catalytic-like coherence effects (including Aberg's catalytic coherence) can only occur without degradation in the presence of infinite-dimensional reference systems; finite-dimensional references forbid such broadcasting of coherence [d48080s0p0]. Quantum reference frames can exhibit entanglement and coherence properties that affect whether subsystems admit separable descriptions and thus influence the role of references in enabling transformations [d117620s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Are coherence creation and coherence distillation irreversible processes, and what fundamental bounds govern their efficiencies?
How do energy conservation and superselection rules limit which coherences (between which energy levels) can be generated by unitaries?
sub_answers.text: Conservation laws forbid generating superpositions of eigenstates of the corresponding conserved quantities by quantum dynamics, thereby limiting which coherences unitaries can create [d48080s0p0]. Such coherence (asymmetry) is a resource that cannot be freely distributed or broadcast in finite-dimensional systems under these conservation constraints [d48080s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What open problems remain about the trade-off between energy cost and achievable coherence in finite-size or single-shot regimes?
How does creating coherence from thermal states affect quantum work extraction and heat engine performance?
sub_answers.text: Consumption or creation of quantum coherence can increase the total extractable quantum work and improve heat-engine efficiency by contributing a coherent part to work and heat in the energy representation [d48321s0p0]. [d48321s0p0] Quantum coherence can boost output work, currents, and efficiency in driven inelastic heat engines, with geometric (Berry-curvature) effects amplified by coherence helping reach maximal performance [d89804s0p0]. [d73955s0p0] Coherence supplied by non-thermal or coherent reservoirs can enable unconventional thermodynamic behaviour (e.g., hybrid refrigeration and efficiencies exceeding standard Carnot bounds) and sets an effective upper bound on performance when used as a resource [d73955s0p0]. [d48321s0p0] An information-driven heat engine's extractable work is limited by the amount of quantum coherence even when no classical thermodynamic cost is present, so coherence directly bounds what thermodynamic protocols can achieve [d48321s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What advantages does coherence provide in quantum sensing, metrology, or information-processing tasks?
sub_answers.text: Quantum coherence directly enhances metrological resolution and Fisher information, so treating coherence as a finite resource allows optimization of sensing performance [d65004s0p0]. [d94966s0p0] Coherence and entanglement can improve estimator performance in quantum Gaussian sensing and can boost advantages in multivariate quantum estimation strategies such as James–Stein approaches and postselective metrology [d94966s0p0]. [d124546s0p0] Long single-qubit coherence times and good optical interfaces (e.g., in diamond color centers) make coherent states valuable for quantum information processing, distributed quantum computing, sensing and metrology applications [d124546s0p0]. [d40070s0p0] Coherently controllable solid-state defects (like SiV centers) with favorable coherence and optical properties are promising probes and quantum-memory elements that leverage coherence for sensing and QIP tasks [d40070s0p0].

What is a thermal (Gibbs) quantum state and how is it defined in statistical mechanics?
sub_answers.text: A thermal (Gibbs) quantum state is the equilibrium state a small system approaches when it exchanges conserved quantities like heat and particles with a bath, and it is described by the grand canonical ensemble in statistical mechanics [d30255s0p0]. Tracing out an appropriate microcanonical ensemble for a system-and-bath composite yields the system's thermal state, which serves as the equilibrium point of typical dynamics and is characterized by complete passivity in resource-theoretic derivations [d30255s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How is quantum coherence formally defined and quantified (e.g., l1 norm, relative entropy of coherence)?
What is a unitary protocol in quantum thermodynamics and how does it act on a closed system?
What are the standard thermodynamic constraints relevant to quantum state transformations (e.g., conservation laws, second law formulations)?
What general statements relate coherence creation to changes in free energy or entropy in closed quantum operations?
What classes of unitary operations (global versus energy-conserving) can generate coherence from diagonal thermal states?
sub_answers.text: Coherence can be generated either by arbitrary global (system-plus-ancilla) unitaries or, under thermodynamic constraints, only by energy-preserving (thermal) unitaries acting jointly on system and bath; thermal operations are implemented by an energy-preserving system–bath unitary and are covariant and Gibbs-preserving [d33873s0p0][d128220s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What is the role of system Hamiltonian eigenbasis and off-diagonal unitary matrix elements in creating coherence?
sub_answers.text: Coherences are defined relative to the system Hamiltonian eigenbasis, and coherences between different energy levels are constrained by thermodynamic (energy-conservation) conditions [d128220s0p0][d87966s0p0]. The elementary amplitudes for coherence transfer under an energy-preserving unitary are expressed as inner products of bath-weighted vectors associated with total-energy shells, so the off-diagonal (energy-noncommuting) components of the joint unitary determine whether those inner products (and thus coherence transfers) can be nonzero or saturated [d128220s0p0].

Do the second law and resource-theoretic generalized free-energy inequalities (e.g., family of Rényi/free-energy monotones, thermo-majorization constraints, or Jarzynski/Crooks-type relations) categorically forbid generating quantum coherence without net work input, and which precise formulations (thermal operations, Gibbs-preserving maps, or catalytic thermal operations) provide the tightest no-go statements?

What specific roles do catalysts, coherence reservoirs (including embezzling states or bounded-reference frames), and explicit phase reference frames play in enabling transitions that would otherwise violate symmetry/thermodynamic constraints—what are the debated definitions, necessary properties (size, fidelity, energy spectrum), and demonstrated counterexamples in the literature?

Is there an intrinsic irreversibility between coherence formation (creating off-diagonal elements from incoherent/Gibbs states) and coherence distillation (extracting a standard coherent resource), what are the proven conversion rates or single-shot bounds (e.g., relative entropy of coherence, coherence cost vs distillable coherence), and which fundamental inequalities determine their efficiency gaps?

Under strict energy conservation and superselection rules (time-translation symmetry), how do commutation relations with the total Hamiltonian and degeneracy structure constrain which off-diagonal coherences (between which pairs or manifolds of energy eigenstates) can be produced by energy-preserving unitaries or allowed operations?
sub_answers.text: Coherence-transfer amplitudes under energy-preserving unitaries can be expressed as inner products of bath-weighted vectors associated with total-energy shells, tying allowed coherences to the energy-resolution structure of the joint system–bath [d128220s0p0]. Saturation of the Cauchy–Schwarz bounds for an elementary coherence transfer requires those bath-weighted vectors to be collinear, and a single global energy-preserving unitary cannot in general make the distinct vectors for multiple transfers all collinear simultaneously [d128220s0p0]. Trace- and Gibbs-preservation impose additional phase-closure conditions and polygon inequalities that further restrict which off-diagonal coherences between energy eigenstate pairs or manifolds can be realized by allowed operations [d128220s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In what precise ways does quantum coherence enhance sensing, metrology, or information-processing performance—e.g., improvements in Fisher information, precision scaling (standard quantum limit vs Heisenberg limit), clock stability, readout fidelity, or algorithmic speedups—and what explicit tasks and metrics demonstrate those advantages?
sub_answers.text: Quantum coherence increases Fisher information and can enable Heisenberg-like scaling in estimation, giving quantum Fisher information that scales as N^2 for GHZ-like states used in metrology [d100142s0p0][d116756s0p0]. Coherence-augmented sensing protocols can extend spectral precision beyond the sensor's coherence time, producing a frequency-estimation precision that scales as T^{-3/2} for classical oscillating fields and achieving intrinsic frequency resolution down to 607 μHz in a single-spin diamond magnetometer [d38271s0p0]. Entanglement and engineered coherent dynamics yield unconditional metrological advantage quantified by enhanced Fisher information per photon, e.g., a 5.8(1)-fold Fisher-information gain above the shot-noise limit in a robust photonic scheme [d82701s0p0]. Sequential coherent-control strategies improve quantum Fisher information per dose in lossy interferometry, enabling higher precision under dose constraints compared to classical or parallel strategies [d125378s0p0]. Combining coherence-based critical-state preparation with conventional phase encoding adds interference terms that increase quantum Fisher information and enable near–Cramér–Rao-limit readout fidelity improvements in sensing protocols [d91081s0p0].

From a resource-theoretic perspective, how does the ability to generate coherence from thermal inputs change operational quantities such as coherence cost, distillable coherence, coherence of formation, conversion rates between coherence and entanglement, impacts on channel capacities for quantum communication, and implications for fault-tolerant error-correction thresholds?

Provide the precise expressions for work and energy change (e.g., W = Tr[H(Uρ_GU† − ρ_G)]), clarify sign conventions, and state any equivalent formulations in terms of changes in expected energy, internal energy, or provided/returned work in a thermally isolated process.

Which explicit relationships and inequalities tie standard coherence measures (for example, relative entropy of coherence, l1-norm of coherence, and coherence as distance to the dephased state) to work, free-energy change, or extractable work under unitary evolution starting from thermal states? Request exact formulas, equalities or lower/upper bounds, and conditions under which they hold (temperature dependence, additivity, asymptotic limits).

In protocols that create coherence while obeying energy-conservation constraints, how are ancillas, catalytic systems, and correlated reference frames employed? Ask for concrete protocol forms (energy-preserving global unitaries with ancilla, catalytic coherence examples, embezzling-like reference frames), necessary resource states, and how correlations or catalyst reuse are handled to satisfy strict conservation laws.

Do laws like the second law of thermodynamics, free energy monotones (e.g., non-equilibrium free energy, generalized free energy families), or resource-theory constraints forbid generating quantum coherence without net work input, and which formal statements (e.g., free energy inequalities, fluctuation theorems, passivity results) are applicable?
sub_answers.text: Monotones based on free energy constrain thermodynamic state transformations and single out free-energy-like quantities as measures of athermality that must not increase under the allowed free operations [d36719s0p0]. Fluctuation-dissipation relations link the amount of free energy dissipated in optimal thermodynamic distillation processes to the free-energy fluctuations of the initial state, including for states with coherence between energy eigenstates, providing formal inequalities that bound performance up to second-order asymptotics in the number of systems processed [d67667s0p0]. A resource-theoretic formulation without a background thermal reservoir shows thermodynamic state space is constrained to an energy–entropy diagram where entropy and average energy classify states and hence restrict possible transformations, which functions as a convex constraint on creating resources like coherence under thermodynamic rules [d33228s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which experimental protocols have demonstrably generated quantum coherence starting from thermal or near-thermal initial states in platforms such as liquid-state NMR, trapped-ion chains, and superconducting transmon/cQED devices? For each platform, list the control techniques used (e.g., resonant microwave pulses, sideband drives, joint unitary operations, measurement-based preparation), the reported initial effective temperatures or population distributions, the coherence measures reported (l1-norm, relative entropy of coherence, off-diagonal density-matrix elements), typical fidelities and decoherence times, and key experimental references or figures showing the coherence creation.

From a resource-theory perspective, what are the operational consequences of creating coherence from thermal states for quantum communication and quantum error correction? Specifically: how does coherence cost or gain affect channel capacities, entanglement generation rates, distillable coherence versus coherence of formation under classes of operations (IO, SIO, MIO), the possibility of catalytic coherence, and concrete impacts on error-correcting thresholds or syndrome extraction when ancillas begin in thermal states? Provide references to formal bounds and any applied analyses linking coherence measures to communication or QEC performance.

How does converting thermal (Gibbs or near-Gibbs) states into states with quantum coherence change equilibration dynamics and performance of quantum thermodynamic protocols? Ask for results on how added coherence modifies relaxation rates, steady-state populations, work extraction in single-shot and many-copy regimes (including corrections to free energy and non-equilibrium free energy frameworks), effects on fluctuation theorems and entropy production, and examples in autonomous engines or thermalization experiments that quantify coherence contributions to extracted work or to deviations from canonical equilibration.
sub_answers.text: Quantum coherence can change the effective lower bounds on energetic cost during information erasure, with an entropic bound tighter for sufficiently mixed initial states and a thermodynamic (fluctuation-related) bound tighter for high-purity initial states; this relation holds irrespective of whether coherence is present except in pure phase-relaxation dynamics where the thermodynamic bound is tighter unless initial coherence is zero [d75114s0p0]. Quantum information erasure that generates system--reservoir correlations inevitably accompanies an extra, constant energy dissipation term tied to those correlations, introducing an additional energetic cost beyond the usual bounds [d75114s0p0]. Dynamical instability increases decoherence rates and thus alters equilibration: in the Ehrenfest regime, greater classical instability (larger Lyapunov exponent) leads to faster loss of off-diagonal terms, which will speed changes in relaxation of coherence and affect thermalization timescales [d17998s0p0]. The remote creation of coherence in spin chains depends on temperature and chain length: coherence intensity vanishes as chain length grows and cannot become significant unless polarization is large, linking initial thermal populations to achievable coherence and hence to equilibration and protocol performance in extended systems [d28433s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Provide the definition of a thermal (Gibbs) quantum state used in statistical mechanics and quantum thermodynamics, including its mathematical form ρ = e^{-βH}/Z, the role of the Hamiltonian, inverse temperature β, and the partition function Z, and discuss any equivalent formulations (e.g., maximum-entropy derivation).
sub_answers.text: A thermal (Gibbs) quantum state is the canonical ensemble ρ = e^{-βH}/Z, where H is the system Hamiltonian, β is the inverse temperature, and Z = Tr[e^{-βH}] is the partition function that normalizes the state [d111916s0p0] [d70838s0p0]. The Hamiltonian H determines the energy eigenbasis and energies that enter the exponential weighting e^{-βH}, hence specifying the state's dependence on the system's energy spectrum [d70838s0p0]. The inverse temperature β parametrizes the thermal population bias: larger β concentrates weight on lower-energy eigenstates while β→0 yields the maximally mixed state; the partition function Z ensures unit trace and encodes thermodynamic potentials [d70838s0p0] [d137949s0p0]. Equivalently, the Gibbs state can be derived from Jaynes' maximum-entropy principle as the state of maximal von Neumann entropy subject to a fixed average energy constraint, and it also arises as the reduced state of a microcanonical state on system plus large environment (mean-force or reduced Gibbs perspective) [d111916s0p0] [d70838s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Explain how quantum coherence is defined in the resource-theory approach: specify the incoherent basis concept, give formal coherence measures (l1-norm of coherence, relative entropy of coherence), and state their mathematical formulas and operational interpretations.

Describe what is meant by a unitary protocol acting in quantum thermodynamics: characterize unitary operations on a closed system (global vs subsystem unitaries), how they transform density matrices (ρ -> UρU†), which quantities they preserve (spectrum, von Neumann entropy), and typical classes of thermodynamic unitaries (energy-conserving unitaries, thermal operations).

List and explain the standard thermodynamic constraints and conservation laws that limit quantum state transformations: energy conservation, particle-number or other conserved charges, the second law in various formulations (entropy non-decrease, free-energy monotones, thermomajorization), and any additional resource-theory constraints (e.g., catalytic or allowed ancilla conditions).

What general inequalities or theorems connect the generation or modification of coherence under closed quantum operations to changes in free energy or entropy? Cite relations such as the work cost of creating coherence, bounds involving relative entropy of coherence and non-equilibrium free energy differences, and statements about entropy production under dephasing versus coherent transformations.

Which broad categories of unitary operations (for example, arbitrary global unitaries, energy-preserving unitaries that commute with total Hamiltonian, or unitaries constrained to block-diagonal energy sectors) are capable of producing off-diagonal coherence when applied to initial Gibbs/diagonal thermal states?
sub_answers.text: Unitary operators that do not preserve the diagonal algebra (i.e., are not in the class characterized as diagonal-preserving or block-diagonal-preserving) can produce off-diagonal coherence when acting on diagonal (thermal) states [d33873s0p0]. Energy-preserving unitaries appearing in thermal operations can produce coherence but their coherence-transfer amplitudes are constrained by energy-resolved Stinespring structure and inner-product (Cauchy–Schwarz) bounds, so not all transfers are simultaneously achievable [d128220s0p0]. Unitaries that explicitly preserve block-diagonal or tensor-product algebras will not create coherence across those blocks and thus cannot produce off-diagonal elements between those blocks [d33873s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does expressing the system in the Hamiltonian eigenbasis clarify the necessary structure of a unitary's matrix elements (specific nonzero off-diagonal couplings between energy eigenstates, selection rules) for generating coherences, and how do degeneracies or level spacings affect which matrix elements are relevant?
sub_answers.text: Expressing the system in the Hamiltonian eigenbasis lets one write elementary coherence-transfer amplitudes as inner products of bath-weighted vectors associated with total-energy shells, so the relevant nonzero unitary matrix elements are those coupling the specific energy-eigenstate pairs whose total energies match allowed shell transitions [d128220s0p0]. Saturation of Cauchy–Schwarz bounds for those inner products requires the associated bath vectors to be collinear, which imposes selection-like constraints on which matrix elements can reach maximal transfer simultaneously [d128220s0p0]. Degeneracies or level spacings enter through the total-energy shells and can change which matrix elements (i.e., which eigenstate pairs) lie in the same shell and thus which couplings are relevant or constrained by phase-closure and polygon inequalities [d128220s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Given an isolated quantum system initially in a thermal (Gibbs) state, how is the work or energy change associated with applying a unitary U computed explicitly (e.g., via expectation values of H before and after, ΔE = Tr[H(UρU†−ρ)]), and how do initial state populations enter that calculation?

What precise relationships or equations have been derived that link quantitative coherence measures (such as relative entropy of coherence, l1-norm of coherence, or off-diagonal Frobenius norm) to thermodynamic quantities like work, nonequilibrium free energy change ΔF, or extractable work under unitary operations starting from thermal states?

In protocols that generate coherence while obeying energy conservation, how are auxiliary systems used—specifically, what roles do explicit ancilla systems with given Hamiltonians, catalytic states that remain unchanged, or correlated/phase reference frames (e.g., coherent or squeezed reference systems) play, and what constraints or resource-accounting rules (like conservation of total energy and return-to-initial-state conditions for catalysts) govern their use?
sub_answers.text: Ancillary (bath) systems enter via an energy-resolved Stinespring representation: coherence transfers are produced by a single energy-preserving system–bath unitary acting on system plus ancilla, so the ancilla (bath) Hilbert space and its energy shells determine the bath-weighted vectors appearing in coherence-transfer amplitudes [d128220s0p0]. Characterizations of bipartite unitaries that generate operations preserving diagonal or block-diagonal algebras show that some unitaries induce the desired system map independently of the ancilla state, indicating specific structural roles for ancillas in preserving or enabling coherences [d33873s0p0]. Trace- and Gibbs-preservation constraints on thermal operations impose additional phase-closure conditions and polygon inequalities on allowed coherence transfers, which function as resource-accounting rules linking the allowed ancilla-assisted transformations to conservation of total energy and Gibbs-preserving requirements [d128220s0p0].
